tagline.text: A moss-covered 70 m waterfall hidden in the forests of Luisiana, Laguna

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–February, the cool dry season (the falls flow strongest in the rainy season)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱400~900 (round-trip transport from Manila, registration and a shared guide fee)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) — about 3 hours by road

children.text: Hulugan Falls is a waterfall about 70 m high in the forest of Luisiana, Laguna, roughly 120 km southeast of Manila. Water streams down a moss-covered rock face, and with a short downhill trek led by a guide plus the nearby Talay and Hidden Falls you can do it all in one day.

Hulugan Falls lies deep in the forest of Barangay San Salvador in Luisiana, Laguna. It is about 120 km southeast of Manila, so by public transport you can go and return in a day if you leave early in the morning. Guides give its height as about 70 m or more, and the water pours in several streams down a tall, moss-covered rock face, which makes it a very photogenic waterfall. Compared with better-known falls such as Pagsanjan or Daranak, it still feels like a small attraction run by the villagers.

The way to the falls starts at the registration post. After registering near the arch at the entrance of San Salvador, you ride a tricycle to the jump-off point and walk from there with a local guide. A guide is described as mandatory, and since the path is slippery and has forks, it is necessary for safety as well. The traditional trail takes about 30–45 minutes one way, is longer but safer, and passes Hidden Falls and Talay Falls on the way. The shortcut takes only about 15–20 minutes going down, but it is steep and slippery and tiring on the way back up.

Fees differ a little by source. A 2021 blog listed a registration fee of ₱40 and a guide fee of ₱500 (up to 10 people), while a 2025 guide listed a registration fee of ₱50, an environmental fee of ₱40 and a guide fee of ₱500 (up to 5 people). The most accurate approach is to check the current prices at the registration post when you arrive and to bring cash. There are almost no ATMs or card payments nearby. What to bring is simple: light clothes that can get wet, trekking sandals or shoes with good grip, a change of clothes and a towel, water and snacks, a waterproof pouch, and a plastic bag for trash. There are almost no shops around the falls, so it is best to bring your own food. An umbrella is a nuisance when it rains, so bring a thin raincoat instead. Because this is a village-run attraction, pay the set registration and guide fees and follow the route and rules your guide gives you; that is how you help protect the village and the forest.

The charm of this waterfall is that the path is not very rough, yet you get the atmosphere of forest and stream all at once. In the rainy season the flow is rich and the falls are magnificent, but the path is muddy and the water turns cloudy after heavy rain. In the dry season the flow can shrink, so check recent social media posts for the water level before you visit. In any season it is crowded on weekends, so weekdays are recommended. Luisiana lies at the eastern end of Laguna close to Quezon province, and the road to the falls passes small villages, rice fields and coconut groves, so the journey itself is part of the sight. While you walk down from the village entrance to the falls, the sound of the stream and birdsong alternate, and you may meet locals selling simple drinks and snacks along the way. Going down slowly without rushing and enjoying the atmosphere of the forest is the best way to enjoy this waterfall.

blocks.title: A Moss-Covered Waterfall About 70 m High

children.text: Guides describe it as a tall waterfall of about

or more. Water streaming down the moss-covered rock face blends with the forest and photographs beautifully. You can swim in the pool below the falls, but watch out for the current and slippery rocks. In the rainy season the volume is large and the spray is big, while in the dry season the water thins and the texture of the moss on the rock face shows better.

You register for your visit near the arch at the village entrance and are assigned a guide. Because tourism income goes back to the village, it is good to pay the registration and guide fees honestly. The guides are local residents, so they tell you not only the way but also stories of the village and safety rules.

blocks.title: A Resting Spot Below the Falls and Photo Points

children.text: Many visitors eat lunch and rest on the rocky area in front of the falls. To capture the whole waterfall, shoot vertically from a little distance, and when close up use a waterproof pouch so the spray does not wet your camera. The light is softer in late morning or early afternoon than at midday.

items.title: One-Day Plan
items.subtitle: Trekking to the falls from Manila

children.text: Take a bus from Buendia or Cubao in Manila to Santa Cruz (Laguna). It takes about 2.5–3 hours.
In Santa Cruz, take a jeepney toward Lucban or Lucena and get off at San Salvador.
Register at the village registration post and get a guide.
Ride a tricycle to the jump-off point and go down the traditional trail with your guide, stopping at Hidden Falls and Talay Falls.
Have lunch, swim and take photos at Hulugan Falls.
Begin the climb back up. One guide recommends starting to climb up before 3–4 PM at the latest.
After heavy rain the path is slippery and the water can rise, so shorten or postpone your plans.

items.subtitle: Leave at dawn, home in the afternoon

Arrive at the San Salvador registration post, park, register and arrange a guide.
Go down the traditional trail with your guide, looking around Hidden and Talay Falls.
Enjoy swimming and photos at Hulugan Falls and have a snack.
Climb back up, shower and change, and have lunch in the village.
On the way home, stop at Pagsanjan or Lucban to finish the day.

Hulugan Falls feels different in the dry and rainy seasons. December to February is relatively cool and good for walking, and it is the period recommended by guides. One review says the flow can thin in the dry season, so if the grandeur of the falls matters, you can also pick a clear day at the start of the rainy season in June–July or toward its end in November. Even then the path is wet, so pay attention to your footwear.
The rainy season (June–November) brings plenty of water, but the path is slippery and the stream crossings are dangerous. Do not go on days of heavy rain or during a typhoon.
On weekends visitors crowd in and the wait for registration and a guide can be long, so weekdays are much more relaxed. One guide gives an example schedule with a return to the village at 4 PM.

There is little lodging near the falls. Most people make it a day trip, and to stay overnight you look for lodging in Santa Cruz or toward Pagsanjan. One guide says camping in the village is also possible for ₱100. If you want to stay overnight, a common plan is to book a mid-range hotel in Santa Cruz and add the Pagsanjan Falls canoe ride the next day. To camp near the falls, first ask at the village registration post whether it is allowed and what it costs.
There are almost no restaurants, so bring a packed lunch, water and snacks. There may be a small shop at the village entrance, but the choice is limited.

If you leave Manila at dawn, you can reach the falls before lunch and be out of the village before sunset. On the way back, a simple meal in Santa Cruz town before the bus is a sensible plan. If you have time, you can extend the trip to two days by adding nearby Pagsanjan Falls or Lucban on the same route.

Get a local guide at the San Salvador village registration point. Past reports give different group limits; confirm how many guides your group needs, extra charges for each waterfall and the last registration time before setting out.
Wear non-slip trekking sandals or shoes and clothes that can get wet.
Bring plenty of cash in small bills. There are no ATMs.
Put your phone and wallet in a waterproof pouch.
Go on a weekday if you can. Weekends are crowded.
Allowing for both the trip down and the climb back, start early and return to the village before dark.
Leave Manila at early dawn. You need to reach the village before the jeepneys from Santa Cruz stop running.
Having lots of small bills makes it easier to pay for jeepneys, tricycles and registration.
If you have companions you can split the guide fee, so the more people, the lower the cost per person.
Do not go after heavy rain or during a typhoon, as the path is slippery and flash floods can occur.
The shortcut is steep and slippery and tiring on the way back. If you are not very fit, choose the traditional trail.

Do not climb the rocks near the falls, and avoid strong currents. Especially on wet days, if your guide says to turn back, do so. If you are with children or older people, use only the traditional trail and leave plenty of rest time on the way up.
Fees and hours differ by source, so confirm them locally.
Ask permission before photographing villagers or their homes.
The forest gets dark early in the late afternoon, so start climbing back up before 3–4 PM at the latest.
When swimming in the falls' pool, ask your guide first which parts are shallow and which are deep, and do not go into deep water alone.
